'''Robert Otto Pohl''' (December 17, 1929 – August 30, 2024) was a German-American physicist, specialized in [[condensed matter physics]] topics such as [[Amorphous solid|amorphous solids]], [[glass]], [[thermal conductivity]], and [[thin films]],<ref name=aip>{{cite web|title=Robert O. Pohl|website=Physics History Network, AIP (American Institute of Physics)|url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11608012.html}}</ref> who was the Goldwin Smith Emeritus Professor of Physics at [[Cornell University]]. He developed the [[3ω-method]], widely used to measure thermal conductivities.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tong |first=Tao |last2=Majumdar |first2=Arun |date=2006-10-05 |title=Reexamining the 3-omega technique for thin film thermal characterization |url=https://pubs.aip.org/aip/rsi/article-abstract/77/10/104902/1017864/Reexamining-the-3-omega-technique-for-thin-film?redirectedFrom=fulltext |journal=Review of Scientific Instruments |volume=77 |issue=10 |pages=104902 |doi=10.1063/1.2349601 |issn=0034-6748|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He is also known for showing that thermal properties of [[glass]] are different from [[Crystal|crystalline solids]] at low temperatures.<ref name=":0" />

==Biography==
Pohl was born in [[Göttingen]] in 1929.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Robert Pohl, innovator in condensed matter physics, dies at 94 {{!}} Cornell Chronicle |url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2024/09/robert-pohl-innovator-condensed-matter-physics-dies-94 |access-date=2025-04-28 |website=news.cornell.edu |language=en}}</ref> His father was the physicist [[Robert Wichard Pohl]],<ref name=":0" /> whose maternal grandfather was {{ill|Wichard Lange|de}} (1826–1884), a member of the [[Hamburg Parliament]]. After completing undergraduate study at the [[University of Freiburg]], Pohl matriculated as a graduate student at the [[University of Erlangen–Nuremberg]]. There he graduated with a ''[[Diplom]]'' (M.S.) in 1955 and a doctorate in 1957 and worked as an assistant in physics for the academic year 1957–1958.<ref name=aip/> He immigrated to the United States in 1958. 

At [[Cornell University]], he was a research associate from 1958 to 1960, an [[assistant professor]] from 1960 to 1963, an associate professor from 1963 to 1968, a full professor from 1968 to 2000, and Goldwin Smith Emeritus Professor of Physics from 2000 to 2024. He held visiting appointments at [[RWTH Aachen University]] (1964), the [[University of Stuttgart]] (1966–1967), [[LMU Munich]], the [[University of Konstanz]], the [[University of Regensburg]], New Zealand's [[University of Canterbury]], China's [[Tongji University]], and the [[Nuclear Research Centre Julich|Nuclear Research Center Jülich]].<ref name=Cornell>{{cite web |url=https://physics.cornell.edu/robert-pohl |title=Robert Pohl |website=Department of Physics, Cornell University}}</ref>

=== Research ===
Robert O. Pohl has done research on experimental investigations of glass and glassy materials,<ref name="casnl-spr85">{{cite news |date=Spring 1985 |title=Faculty Notes |work=Cornell Arts & Sciences Newsletter |publisher=Cornell University |page=7}}</ref> as well as heat transport and lattice transport behavior in crystalline solids and in amorphous solids, structure of glass, cryogenic techniques, and energy problems.<ref name="Cornell" />

With R. C. Zeller, Pohl worked on glass at low temperatures. They showed in 1971 that glasses behave similarly at low temperature but do not follow the [[Debye model]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ramos |first=M. A. |date=2020-02-01 |title=Are universal “anomalous” properties of glasses at low temperatures truly universal? |url=https://pubs.aip.org/aip/ltp/article-abstract/46/2/104/252791/Are-universal-anomalous-properties-of-glasses-at?redirectedFrom=fulltext |journal=Low Temperature Physics |volume=46 |issue=2 |pages=104–110 |doi=10.1063/10.0000527 |issn=1063-777X|arxiv=2001.04487 }}</ref>

His doctoral students included [[Venkatesh Narayanamurti]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Robert Otto Pohl, Ph.D. |url=https://academictree.org/physics/peopleinfo.php?pid=98715 |website=Physics Tree}}</ref>

Springer published Robert Wichard Pohl's 3-volume edition of ''Einführung in die Physik'' (vol. 1, ''Mechanik und Akustik'', 1930; vol. 2, ''Elektrizitätslehre'', 1927; vol. 3, 1940, ''Optik'') with many later editions and a 2-volume edition edited by Klaus Lüders and Robert O. Pohl (vol. 1, ''Mechanik, Akustik und Wärmelehre'', 19th edition, 2004; vol. 2, 22nd edition, 2006). Robert O. Pohl added videos of demonstration experiments for the latest editions.<ref>{{cite web |year=2003 |title=Physikalische Experimente nach Robert Wichard Pohl (1884 - 1976) (Physical experiments according to Robert Wichard Pohl) |url=https://av.tib.eu/series/152 |website=TIB (Technische Informationsbibliothek) AV-Portal}} The German National Library of Science and Technology (TIB), in collaboration with the Hasso Plattner Institute (HPI), developed the AV Portal, which is a user-oriented platform for scientific and technological videos.</ref>

Pohl died in [[Göttingen]], Germany on August 30, 2024, at the age of 94.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Robert Pohl, innovator in condensed matter physics, dies at 94 |url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2024/09/robert-pohl-innovator-condensed-matter-physics-dies-94 |access-date=2024-09-10 |website=Cornell Chronicle |language=en}}</ref>

==Pohl's opinions on nuclear waste disposal==
In addition to his main research interests, Robert O. Pohl was concerned about radioactive waste disposal and its effects on the environment and human health.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Pohl, Robert O.|title=Land-use for Nuclear and for Solar Energy|journal=Environmental Conservation|volume=4|issue=4|year=1977|pages=289–290|doi=10.1017/S0376892900026217 |bibcode=1977EnvCo...4..289P |s2cid=85774778 |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/environmental-conservation/article/abs/landuse-for-nuclear-and-for-solar-energy/3BD6AE09D10A94EB4652718547754E79|url-access=subscription}}</ref> During the [[Presidency of Jimmy Carter|Carter administration]] he served on a Presidential advisory committee on nuclear waste disposal.<ref>{{cite web|title=Robert O. Pohl papers, 1973-1998|website=Division of Rare and Manuscript Collections, Cornell University Library|url=https://rmc.library.cornell.edu/EAD/htmldocs/RMA03253.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040326091812/http://rmc.library.cornell.edu/EAD/htmldocs/RMA03253.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=March 26, 2004}}</ref>

In a 1982 article published in ''Physics Today'', Pohl wrote:<ref>{{cite journal|author=Pohl, R.O.|date=December 1982|title=Debate on radioactive waste disposal. Will it stay put?|journal=Physics Today|volume=35|issue=12|pages=37–45|doi=10.1063/1.2914882|bibcode=1982PhT....35l..37P }}</ref>
{{blockquote|In discussing adequate protection from the nuclear waste, the proper yardstick, in my opinion, is not how many people will be killed by it on a statistical basis (sometimes even expressed as the number of cancer fatalities per megawatt-year of electrical energy produced). Rather, the point is whether we want to impose on future generations the need to live permanently with radiation monitors, something we do not have to do right now—apart from some unfortunate exceptions. In my opinion, we should make every effort to avoid subjecting our descendants to this additional concern. This would require find permanently safe disposal methods for all forms of radioactive wastes, since any disposal of long-lived radioactive species in shallow landfills, or through ocean dumping, as is currently practiced for the many of low-level waste arising in the nuclear fuel cycle, would be unacceptable.<ref>{{cite book|editor=Hafemeister, David|editor2=Levi, Barbara Goss|editor-link2=Barbara Goss Levi|title=Physics and Nuclear Arms Today ''(reprints of articles published in'' Physics Today'')''|year=1991|chapter=''Debate on nuclear waste disposal: Will it stay put?'' by Pohl|pages=207 & 210–217|publisher=Springer |isbn=9780883186404 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Hckys7gpwl4C&pg=PA214}} (quote from p. 214)</ref>}}

== Honors and awards ==
In 1985 he received the [[Oliver E. Buckley Condensed Matter Prize]] for "his pioneering work on low energy excitations in amorphous materials and continued important contributions to the understanding of thermal transport in solids."<ref>{{cite web |title=1985 Oliver E. Buckley Condensed Matter Physics Prize Recipient, Robert O. Pohl |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Pohl&first_nm=Robert&year=1985 |website=American Physical Society (aps.org)}}</ref>  It was considered the highest recognition in condensed matter physics.<ref name="casnl-spr85" />

Pohl was elected in 1972 a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]],<ref>{{cite web |title=APS Fellow Archive, search on year 1972 and institution Cornell University |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1972&unit_id=&institution=Cornell+University |website=American Physical Society}}</ref> in 1984 a fellow of [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]<ref>{{cite web |title=Historic Fellows |url=https://www.aaas.org/fellows/historic |website=American Association for the Advancement of Science}} (Search on "Pohl".)</ref> and in 1999 a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Robert O. Pohl |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/robert-o-pohl-htfvdy/ |website=National Academy of Sciences}}</ref> For the academic year 1973–1974 he was a [[Guggenheim Fellowship|Guggenheim Fellow]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Robert O. Pohl |url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/robert-o-pohl/ |website=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation}}</ref> In 1980 he received the [[Humboldt Research Award|Humboldt US Senior Scientist Award]].<ref name="Cornell" />
